entries.title: Kautilya’s Arthashastra — Book II: The Duties of Superintendents
entries.subtitle: Palm-leaf Sanskrit Treatise on Urban Waterworks, Guilds & Treasury
entries.summary: Detailed administrative manual regulating state granaries, mineral assays, port customs, ecological forest reserves, and municipal fire safety.
entries.originalExcerpt: प्रजासुखे सुखं राज्ञः प्रजानां च हिते हितम्। नात्मप्रियं हितं राज्ञः प्रजानां तु प्रियं हितम्॥
entries.transliteration: Prajāsukhe sukhaṁ rājñaḥ prajānāṁ ca hite hitam | Nātmapriyaṁ hitaṁ rājñaḥ prajānāṁ tu priyaṁ hitam ||
entries.englishTranslation: In the happiness of the subjects lies the sovereign’s happiness; in their welfare lies his welfare. What pleases himself is not the ruler’s good, but whatever pleases his subjects is his true good.
entries.scholarlyAnalysis: Book I & II balance realpolitik fiscal auditing with strict anti-corruption accountability for royal superintendents (Adhyakshas). Notice how civic infrastructure—reservoirs, highway rest-houses, and famine relief—is treated as the foundational pillar of state stability.
entries.historicalContext: Rediscovered in 1905 by R. Shamasastry from a Tanjore palm-leaf manuscript gifted to the Mysore Oriental Library, the Arthashastra preserves fifteen books (Adhikaranas) spanning domestic fiscal law, foreign diplomacy (Mandala theory), and urban engineering.
entries.epigraphicNotes: Written in crisp Sutra-Bhashya prose and concluding Anushtubh verses; technical terms for weights (Drona, Pala) align closely with excavated Mauryan punch-marked coinage and Sohgaura copper-plate granary records.

entries.title: Ashokan Major Rock Edict XII — On Inter-Sect Concord
entries.subtitle: Brahmi-Prakrit Epigraph Advocating Restraint of Speech & Mutual Learning
entries.summary: One of fourteen rock edicts issued across the Mauryan realm urging dialogue across philosophical sects (pasanda) and guarding against self-praise at others’ expense.
entries.originalExcerpt: देवानंपियो पियदसि राजा सवपासंडानि पविजितानि च घरस्थानि च पूजयति दानेन च विविधेन च पूजाय।
entries.transliteration: Devānampiyo Piyadasi rājā savapāsaṁḍāni pavajitāni ca gharasthāni ca pūjayati dānena ca vividhena ca pūjāya.
entries.englishTranslation: King Priyadarshi, Beloved of the Gods, honors all sects—both ascetics and householders—with gifts and manifold honors. Restraint of speech is foundational: one should not extol one’s own sect while disparaging another without reason; concord (samavaya) alone is commendable.
entries.scholarlyAnalysis: Girnar Edict XII remains a landmark constitutional statement in ancient global history. Rather than enforcing state orthodoxy, Ashoka frames pluralism as an active civic discipline requiring careful listening (bahusruta) across communities.
entries.citationAuthor: Emperor Ashoka (Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum Vol. I)
entries.repository: Archaeological Survey of India Epigraphy Division
entries.historicalContext: Carved on the same Junagadh granite-basalt boulder that later received Rudradaman’s Sanskrit inscription (150 CE) and Skandagupta’s reservoir repair record (455 CE), demonstrating over seven centuries of continuous public epigraphic dialogue.
entries.epigraphicNotes: Early western-dialect Brahmi characters incised with deep angular strokes; James Prinsep’s 1837–38 decipherment of these Girnar and Dhauli versions unlocked early Indian chronology.

entries.title: Northern Torana Gateway of the Great Stupa at Sanchi
entries.subtitle: Sandstone Architraves Depicting Jataka Narratives & Royal Processions
entries.displayDate: Core c. 250 BCE; Toranas c. 1st c. BCE
entries.provenance: Sanchi Hill, Raisen District, Madhya Pradesh
entries.summary: Finely sculpted triple-architrave sandstone gateway gifted by ivory carvers of Vidisha, illustrating early aniconic Buddhist visual storytelling.
entries.englishTranslation: Carved and gifted by the ivory-workers’ guild of Vidisha.
entries.scholarlyAnalysis: Donative Brahmi inscriptions along the Sanchi railings prove that monumental stone architecture was funded collectively by merchant guilds, artisans, nuns, and householders alongside royal foundations.
entries.historicalContext: Located just ten kilometers from the prosperous commercial crossroads of ancient Vidisha, Sanchi’s brick core was expanded under the Shungas and Satavahanas with four monumental carved gateways.
entries.epigraphicNotes: Over 800 short Brahmi donative inscriptions cover the crossbars and pillars, preserving names of monastic donors from Ujjain, Mahishmati, and Gandhara.

entries.title: Allahabad Pillar Prashasti of Samudragupta
entries.subtitle: Harishena’s Sanskrit Champu Eulogy on Statecraft & Poetic Patronage
entries.provenance: Originally Kaushambi; relocated to Prayagraj Fort
entries.summary: Composed by court poet and general Harishena, recording Samudragupta’s diplomatic policy of Grahanamokshanugraha (capture, liberation, and alliance) in Dakshinapatha.
entries.englishTranslation: Whose gracious heart is won by submission and homage, whose fame pervades the earth through righteous conquest, and who earned the title King of Poets (Kaviraja) through compositions cherished by the learned.
entries.scholarlyAnalysis: Inscribed directly beneath Ashoka’s own Prakrit edict, the Prayagraj Prashasti visually links Gupta sovereignty with Mauryan antiquity while revealing the nuanced distinction between direct annexation in Aryavarta and tributary diplomacy in the South.
entries.historicalContext: The column serves as a palimpsest of Indian history—bearing Ashoka’s 3rd-century BCE schism edict, Queen Karuvaki’s charity record, Samudragupta’s 4th-century Sanskrit panegyric, and Jahangir’s 1605 CE Persian genealogical engraving.
entries.epigraphicNotes: Composed in ornate Champu (alternating classical Kavya meters such as Sragdhara and Shardulavikridita with rhythmic prose) by Sandhivigrahika Harishena.

entries.title: Mehrauli Iron Pillar Inscription of King Chandra
entries.subtitle: Metallurgical Marvel & Gupta Brahmi Commemorative Verse
entries.summary: Six-line Sanskrit inscription recording the erection of a Garuda standard (dhvaja) celebrating victories in Vanga and across the seven mouths of the Sindhu.
entries.transliteration: Yasyodvartayataḥ pratīpamurasā śatrūnsametyāgatān vaṅgeṣvāhavavartino ’bhilikhitā khaḍgena kīrtirbhuje.
entries.englishTranslation: Upon whose arm fame was inscribed by the sword when he turned back his united foes in battle in the Vanga lands, and who raised this lofty standard of Lord Vishnu upon Mount Vishnupada.
entries.scholarlyAnalysis: Modern materials science confirms that a crystalline iron hydrogen phosphate hydrate passive film—formed from deliberate high-phosphorus slag chemistry—has shielded the 1,600-year-old iron shaft from atmospheric rust.
entries.citationAuthor: Epigraphia Indica Vol. XIV / R. Balasubramaniam
entries.repository: Qutb Complex Heritage Precinct, New Delhi
entries.historicalContext: Identified predominantly with Chandragupta II Vikramaditya, the pillar was originally crowned with a bronze or stone Garuda emblem at a Vishnu sanctuary on Vishnupadagiri (likely Udayagiri in Vidisha) before medieval relocation to Delhi.
entries.epigraphicNotes: Chiseled sharply into forged wrought iron in three classical Sanskrit stanzas, displaying characteristic flat-topped Gupta Brahmi box-headed serifs.

entries.title: Aryabhatiya — Ganitapada & Golapada Folios
entries.subtitle: Compact Sanskrit Verses on Trigonometry, Sine Tables & Earth’s Rotation
entries.provenance: Kusumapura (Pataliputra); preserved in Kerala astronomical lineages
entries.summary: Foundational mathematical astronomy treatise introducing an alphabetic positional numeral encoding (varga-avarga), pi approximation (3.1416), and axial rotation of Earth.
entries.originalExcerpt: अनुलोमगतिर्नौस्थः पश्यत्यचलं विलोमगं यद्वत्। अचलानि भानि तद्वत् समपश्चिमगानि लङ्कायाम्॥
entries.transliteration: Anulomagatirnausthaḥ paśyatyacalaṁ vilomagaṁ yadvat | Acalāni bhāni tadvat samapaścimagāni laṅkāyām ||
entries.englishTranslation: Just as a person in a forward-moving boat sees stationary trees on the bank moving backward, so do the fixed stars appear from Lanka to move uniformly westward while the Earth rotates.
entries.scholarlyAnalysis: Preserved meticulously by the Kerala School of Astronomy and Mathematics centuries after 499 CE, Aryabhata’s verses encapsulate complex trigonometric algorithms in ultra-dense mnemonic meters.
entries.citationAuthor: Aryabhata (Trans. K. S. Shukla & K. V. Sarma)
entries.historicalContext: Aryabhata’s work later stimulated Bhaskara I’s 629 CE commentary, Arabic translations at Baghdad under the title Zij al-Arjabhar, and Madhava of Sangamagrama’s infinite trigonometric series.
entries.epigraphicNotes: Divided into four terse chapters (Gitikapada, Ganitapada, Kalakriyapada, Golapada) totaling 121 Aryā-meter couplets using alphanumeric consonant-vowel place notation.

entries.title: Uttaramerur Inscriptions — The Kudavolai Electoral Charter
entries.subtitle: Granite Temple Wall Constitution Governing Village Assembly Elections
entries.material: Engraved Granite Wall of Vaikuntha Perumal Temple
entries.summary: Remarkable constitutional epigraph detailing thirty wards (kudumbu), candidate eligibility, mandatory asset integrity, and impartial palm-leaf pot selection.
entries.originalExcerpt: முப்பது குடும்பிலும் வெவ்வேறே வாய் ஓலை எழுதிப் பானையிலிட்டுக் குடைவோலை வாங்கி வாரியம் செய்தல்.
entries.transliteration: Muppadu kuḍumbilum vevvēṟē vāy ōlai eḻudip pāṉaiyiliṭṭuk kuḍavōlai vāṅgi vāriyam seydal.
entries.englishTranslation: In each of the thirty wards, the names of eligible candidates shall be written separately on palm-leaf tickets, placed in a pot, and drawn at random by a young boy to constitute the Tank, Garden, and Justice committees.
entries.scholarlyAnalysis: The charter explicitly disqualifies anyone who failed to submit public accounts, took bribes, or committed civic offenses—along with their close kin—establishing one of medieval Asia’s most transparent municipal audit frameworks.
entries.citationAuthor: Parantaka Chola I Epigraph (ASI Annual Report 1904–05)
entries.historicalContext: Issued in the 12th and 14th regnal years of Parantaka Chola I, the second 921 CE resolution refined the 919 CE charter in the presence of royal commissioner Karanjiyan Tattanur Muvendavelan.
entries.epigraphicNotes: Engraved cleanly across dressed granite courses on the adhishthana plinth of the Sabha Mandapa, switching effortlessly from Grantha script for Sanskrit invocations to Tamil prose for procedural bylaws.

entries.title: Brihadisvara Temple (Rajarajeshvaram) — Vimana & Epigraphic Wall
entries.subtitle: Monumental Granite Sanctuary & Comprehensive Royal Ledger
entries.dimensions: Vimana Height 66 m; Monolithic Shikhara 80 tonnes
entries.summary: UNESCO World Heritage granite temple whose plinth walls serve as a stone archive listing dancers, musicians, gold weights, bronze icons, and village endowments.
entries.originalExcerpt: ஸ்வஸ்தி ஸ்ரீ திருமகள் போல பெருநிலச் செல்வியும் தனக்கே உரிமை பூண்டமை மனக்கொள...
entries.transliteration: Svasti Śrī tirumagaḷ pōla perunilac celviyum taṉakkē urimai pūṇḍamai maṉakkoḷa...
entries.englishTranslation: Hail Prosperity! Having taken the Goddess of the Great Earth as his rightful consort like the Goddess of Fortune, Ko Rajakesarivarman Sri Rajarajadeva ordered these royal endowments to be engraved upon stone.
entries.scholarlyAnalysis: Chief architect Kunjara Mallan Rajaraja Perunthachan engineered the hollow tiered vimana without mortar, while temple scribes recorded over 400 temple musicians and 600 administrative personnel with exact daily grain stipends.
entries.citationAuthor: Rajaraja Chola I (South Indian Inscriptions Vol. II)
entries.historicalContext: Funded by agricultural revenues from across Cholamandalam, Sri Lanka, and royal treasuries, Rajarajeshvaram functioned simultaneously as a sacred center, civic bank lending to village assemblies at fixed 12.5% interest, and royal archive.
entries.epigraphicNotes: Opens with Rajaraja’s standardized Meykkirtti (royal historical preface) engraved in crisp 11th-century Chola Tamil paleography along the entire base molding.

entries.title: Tiruvalangadu Copper-Plate Charter of Rajendra Chola I
entries.subtitle: 31 Engraved Copper Plates Joined by Royal Tiger-Fish-Bow Seal
entries.material: Hammered Copper Plates & Cast Bronze Seal Ring
entries.summary: Monumental bilingual charter detailing Solar dynasty myths, Chola victories in Sri Lanka and the Gangetic plains, and tax-free land grant boundaries for temple upkeep.
entries.originalExcerpt: स्वस्ति श्री राजेन्द्रचोलदेवः पलयैयूरिन् कीழ் பழையனூர் திருவாலங்காட்டுடைய மகாதேவர்க்கு தேவதானமாக...
entries.transliteration: Svasti Śrī Rājendracōladevaḥ Paḻaiyaṉūr Tiruvālaṅgāṭṭuḍaiya Mahādēvarkku dēvadānamāga...
entries.englishTranslation: Hail Prosperity! King Rajendra Chola I hereby grants the village of Palaiyanur as a permanent devadana endowment to Lord Mahadeva of Tiruvalangadu, demarcated by perimeter stones and cactus hedges.
entries.scholarlyAnalysis: The massive bronze seal ring bears the Chola tiger emblem flanked by two Pandya fish, the Chera bow, royal parasol, and fly-whisks—visually announcing imperial supremacy across the three crowned Tamil kingdoms.
entries.citationAuthor: Rajendra Chola I (H. Krishna Sastri, SII Vol. III)
entries.historicalContext: Discovered accidentally in 1905 inside a subterranean masonry chamber near Tiruvalangadu, the charter preserves 137 Sanskrit verses by poet Narayana alongside 524 lines of precise Tamil revenue demarcation.
entries.epigraphicNotes: Plates 1–10 carry the Sanskrit Prashasti in ornate Grantha script, while plates 11–31 transition into legal Tamil specifying exact irrigation rights and boundary walks led by a female elephant (Karini-bhramana).

entries.title: Amuktamalyada — Rajaniti Section by Krishnadevaraya
entries.subtitle: Telugu Literary Classic & Royal Manual on Ports, Irrigation & Justice
entries.summary: A poetic synthesis of Vaishnava bhakti and pragmatic Vijayanagara statecraft advising kings to expand irrigation tanks, protect foreign maritime traders, and divide revenue judiciously.
entries.originalExcerpt: విస్తరించి చెఱువుల్ గావించి ధాన్యమ్ము వృద్ధి నొందింపవలయు భూపతి యెపుడు.
entries.transliteration: Vistariñci ceṟuvul gāviñci dhānyammu vṛddhi nondimpavalayu bhūpati yepuḍu.
entries.englishTranslation: A king should ever expand reservoirs and irrigation canals to multiply the harvest of the land, for prosperity rises from water and diligent cultivators.
entries.scholarlyAnalysis: Canto IV (verses 205–285) constitutes a rare first-person treatise authored by a reigning emperor, advocating honest port tariffs so Arab and Portuguese merchants bring horses and jewels rather than fleeing to rival harbors.
entries.historicalContext: Dedicated to Lord Venkateswara of Tirumala during Krishnadevaraya’s triumphant Kalinga campaigns, the work bridges classical Tamil Alwar devotion (Andal’s story) with Telugu Prabandham poetry.
entries.epigraphicNotes: Composed in intricate Champaka-mala and Utpala-mala meters; statecraft maxims recommend dividing royal income into four parts: charity/dharma, personal upkeep, military readiness, and emergency reserve.

entries.title: Vittala Temple Complex — Acoustic Granite Mandapa & Stone Chariot
entries.subtitle: Pinnacle of Vijayanagara Dravidian Stonecraft at Hampi
entries.summary: Famed for its 56 slender clustered granite pillars tuned to produce classical musical notes when tapped, alongside the iconic sculpted Garuda Stone Chariot.
entries.englishTranslation: The Ranga Mandapa of Sri Vittala-deva was constructed within the realm of Vijayanagara for music, dance, and seasonal festivals.
entries.scholarlyAnalysis: Petrographic acoustic testing shows variations in silica density and slender pillar shaft diameters were intentionally carved to sustain resonant harmonics for temple percussion and vocal accompaniment.
entries.historicalContext: Expanded across the reigns of Krishnadevaraya, Achyuta Deva Raya, and Sadasiva Raya, the complex was approached via a 945-meter granite-paved chariot street lined with merchant galleries and stepped water tanks.
entries.epigraphicNotes: More than 25 Kannada and Sanskrit inscriptions on the outer prakara walls document festival endowments by queens, generals, and merchant guilds.

entries.title: Ain-i-Akbari — Gazetteer of Imperial Sciences & Administration
entries.subtitle: Volume III of the Akbarnama by Abu’l-Fazl ibn Mubarak
entries.material: Gold-flecked Sialkoti Paper with Mineral Pigments
entries.summary: Exhaustive 16th-century statistical, fiscal, and cultural survey detailing Mughal mints, Todar Mal’s crop tables, Indian philosophies, music ragas, and Sulh-i-Kul.
entries.originalExcerpt: صلحِ کل اساسِ فرمانروائی است و خردمندِ دادگر همگان را به چشمِ مهر نگرد.
entries.transliteration: Ṣulḥ-i-kul asās-i farmānravā’ī ast va khiradmand-i dādgar hamagān rā ba chashm-i mihr nigarad.
entries.englishTranslation: Universal Peace (Sulh-i-Kul) is the bedrock of governance, wherein a just and discerning sovereign looks upon all communities with an eye of benevolence.
entries.scholarlyAnalysis: Unlike purely dynastic chronicles, Abu’l-Fazl devotes an entire book (Ahwal-i-Hindustan) to sympathetic translations of Samkhya, Nyaya, Vedanta, Jainism, and Indian calendrical astronomy.
entries.citationAuthor: Abu’l-Fazl Allami (Trans. H. Blochmann & H. S. Jarrett)
entries.repository: National Museum Manuscript Collection, New Delhi
entries.historicalContext: Compiled over seven years from provincial archival dispatches submitted by twelve imperial Subahs, recording harvest yields, seasonal prices, artisan wages, and courtly painting guilds.
entries.epigraphicNotes: Royal presentation copies feature lapis lazuli and gold-leaf illuminated sarlauh headpieces framing balanced Nasta‘liq calligraphic columns.

entries.title: Taj Mahal — Pietra Dura & Proportional Charbagh Monograph
entries.subtitle: Makrana Marble Funerary Architecture & Quranic Thuluth Inlay
entries.material: Makrana White Marble inlaid with Jasper, Lapis & Carnelian
entries.summary: Designed under Ustad Ahmad Lahori with calligraphic pietra dura scaling progressively upward so script appears uniform from ground level.
entries.originalExcerpt: بنای رفیع روضه منوره در کنار آب جون به اهتمام استادان هند و ایران انجام یافت.
entries.transliteration: Binā-yi rafī‘-i rawża-yi munawwara dar kinār-i āb-i Jūn ba ihtimām-i ustādān-i Hind u Īrān anjām yāft.
entries.englishTranslation: The lofty edifice of the illuminated garden-tomb on the banks of the Yamuna was brought to completion through the mastery of Indian and Persian artisans.
entries.scholarlyAnalysis: Optical scaling of Amanat Khan’s black-jasper inlaid letters on the Pishtaq arch compensates precisely for viewing perspective from the marble terrace below.
entries.citationAuthor: Ebba Koch (The Complete Taj Mahal) & Padshahnama
entries.historicalContext: Positioned along a sweeping bend of the Yamuna so the riverside terrace catches dawn rose, midday ivory, and moonlit silver light while stabilizing foundations with deep brick-and-stone masonry wells.
entries.epigraphicNotes: Amanat Khan Shirazi signed and dated the inner calligraphic bands (1048 AH / 1638–39 CE), integrating traditional Indian floral motifs (parchin kari) alongside geometric arabesques.

entries.title: Rajavyavaharakosha — State Administrative Lexicon of Shivaji Maharaj
entries.subtitle: Sanskrit-Marathi Dictionary Replacing Courtly Persian Loanwords
entries.provenance: Raigad Fort Court; authored by Raghunath Narayan Hanmante
entries.summary: Commissioned by Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj to standardize administrative, military, naval, and diplomatic vocabulary across Ashta Pradhan chanceries.
entries.englishTranslation: In obedience to the command of Chhatrapati Shivaji, this lexicon of royal administration (Rajavyavaharakosha) was composed by Raghunath Pandit.
entries.scholarlyAnalysis: Organized into ten topical chapters—from Royal Palace (Rajavarga) and Cavalry (Ashvavarga) to Naval Ports (Durga-Nauloka)—the lexicon created terms such as Peshwa→Mukhya Pradhan and Dabir→Sumant.
entries.citationAuthor: Raghunath Narayan Hanmante (Bharata Itihasa Samshodhaka Mandala)
entries.historicalContext: Issued shortly after Shivaji’s 1674 Raigad coronation, the glossary provided a uniform bureaucratic standard adopted across Sahyadri hill forts, Konkan shipyards, and Thanjavur’s Maratha court.
entries.epigraphicNotes: Composed in brisk Anushtubh couplets pairing each outgoing Deccan court term with its Sanskrit-Marathi equivalent so chancery clerks could memorize them rapidly.

entries.title: Adnyapatra — Maratha Royal Edict on Fortresses, Navy & Peasant Welfare
entries.subtitle: Modi-Script Political Treatise by Ramachandrapant Amatya
entries.provenance: Panhala Court of Sambhaji II of Kolhapur
entries.summary: Nine-chapter operational blueprint distilling Shivaji’s administrative doctrines on hill-fort logistics, maritime trade protection, merchant fairness, and agrarian ecology.
entries.originalExcerpt: गड हेच राज्य, गड हेच राजलक्ष्मी, गड हेच खजिना, गड हेच सैन्याचे बळ.
entries.transliteration: Gaḍ hec rājya, gaḍ hec rājalakṣmī, gaḍ hec khajinā, gaḍ hec sainyāce baḷ.
entries.englishTranslation: Forts are the very core of the kingdom; forts are royal prosperity; forts are the treasury and the strength of the army. Even a single mango or jackfruit tree grown by a peasant must never be felled for timber without consent.
entries.scholarlyAnalysis: Chapter 8 on naval strategy and maritime merchants warns against coercing traders, noting that commerce enriches ports only when merchants feel secure in their property and customs rates.
entries.historicalContext: Written by veteran minister Ramachandrapant Amatya—who had served directly under Shivaji Maharaj, Sambhaji, and Rajaram—providing an authentic bridge between 17th-century Swarajya governance and the 18th-century Confederacy.
entries.epigraphicNotes: Preserved in unbroken Modi cursive script on hand-burnished Junnar/Daulatabad paper; each chapter closes with practical inspection checklists for fort commanders (Havaldars and Sabnis).
